## Q1 | Economic Sudoku Sells

<!-- Editor. Q1 is new, written 2026-11-09 so the class has an exercise part it can do early, before the Profit section (E2_Storyboard_Revision.md, Open for Taylor 6, asks for a card that reads q* and profit off known curves). The firm is Exercise E1's Economic Sudoku table with its blanks filled in (A = 60, B = 90, C = 100, D = 130, E = 140), so the Exercises keep one firm across Part E. The prices 135 and 100 are mine: 135 sits between the marginal costs 130 and 140 and gives a small profit, 100 sits between 90 and 130 and gives a loss that is smaller than the fixed cost. Strike the question if the exercise should be the toffee story alone. -->

The firm from Exercise E1 sells in a competitive market, so it takes the market price as given. Its costs are below, with the blanks from last time filled in.

::: {.table style=grid inset=6pt columns="auto 72pt 72pt 72pt 72pt" valign=middle}

| **OUTPUT** | **AFC** | **AVC** | **ATC** | **MC** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1** | 120 | 100 | 220 |   |
|   |   |   |   | 80 |
| **2** | 60 | 90 | 150 |   |
|   |   |   |   | 90 |
| **3** | 40 | 90 | 130 |   |
|   |   |   |   | 130 |
| **4** | 30 | 100 | 130 |   |
|   |   |   |   | 140 |
| **5** | 24 | 108 | 132 |   |

:::

a\) The market price is 135 per unit. How many units does the firm produce, and what is its profit?

 

Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Profit: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

b\) The market price falls to 100 per unit. How many units does the firm produce now, and what is its profit? Should it keep operating in the short run?

 

Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Profit: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Keep operating? \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

c\) Firms like this one enter the market when there is profit to be made and exit when there is a loss. What price does the market settle at in the long run?

 

Long-run price: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: solution

<!-- Editor. The numbers follow from the Exercise E1 table and its key (TC 220, 300, 390, 520, 660 at 1 to 5 units; FC 120). The rule used is the discrete one: add a unit while its marginal cost is below the price. At 135 and 100 no marginal cost equals the price, so there are no ties. -->

**a)** $4$ units, profit $20$. **b)** $3$ units, a loss of $90$; yes, it keeps operating. **c)** $130$ per unit.

**a)** The firm adds a unit as long as the price covers that unit's marginal cost. The marginal costs are $80$, $90$, $130$ and $140$: the second, third and fourth units each cost less than $135$, and the fifth would cost $140 > 135$. So $q^* = 4$. Profit is $TR - TC = 135 \times 4 - 520 = 540 - 520 = 20$, or $q(P - ATC) = 4(135 - 130) = 20$.

**b)** At $100$ the fourth unit is no longer worth making ($130 > 100$), so $q^* = 3$. $TR = 300$, $TC = 390$, so profit is $300 - 390 = -90$, a loss of $90$. The firm keeps operating: the price $100$ is above $AVC = 90$, so each unit more than pays its variable cost and the $30$ left over goes toward the fixed cost. Shutting down would lose the whole fixed cost, $120 > 90$.

The table checks both answers. Profit peaks at $4$ units when the price is $135$ and at $3$ units when it is $100$; shutting down ($q = 0$) loses $120$ either way.

::: {.table style=grid inset=8pt columns="auto 64pt 72pt 72pt 72pt 72pt" fills="r4c3:yellow r3c5:yellow" valign=middle}

| **OUTPUT** | **TC** | **TR at 135** | **Profit** | **TR at 100** | **Profit** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1** | 220 | 135 | −85 | 100 | −120 |
| **2** | 300 | 270 | −30 | 200 | −100 |
| **3** | 390 | 405 | 15 | 300 | −90 |
| **4** | 520 | 540 | 20 | 400 | −120 |
| **5** | 660 | 675 | 15 | 500 | −160 |

:::

**c)** Profit draws firms in and a loss drives them out, and the price only stops moving once profit is zero. Zero profit means $P = ATC$ at the firm's chosen quantity, which happens at the lowest point of the ATC curve, $130$. At $130$ the firm earns nothing at either $3$ or $4$ units ($ATC = 130$ at both, so $TR = TC = 390$ or $520$). At any price above $130$ there is profit and firms enter, pushing the price down; at any price below it there is a loss and firms exit, pushing the price up.

:::

## Q2 | Traditional Toffee Specific Tax

Due to longstanding tradition, all toffees are made the same way, anyone could easily start making them, and the number of toffee makers had been constant over the past couple of years. This changed when the Ministry imposed a specific (*i.e. per-unit*) tax on all toffee sales. Using a couple of graphs to illustrate your answer, explain what happened in the market because of this tax.

::::: solution

<!-- Editor. The story and the two graphs follow Taylor's ink key (../../E_Practice_Bank/Classwork_E2_toffee-tax_sols.pdf): one market graph with the supply curve shifting up by the tax and then in as makers exit, and one firm graph with MC, ATC, the flat price falling to MR₂ and the loss box, ending back at the starting price. The curves drawn are illustrative, mine: D: P = 100 − Q, S: P = Q, a tax of 20, and a maker with MC = q and ATC = q/2 + 1250/q, lowest at q = 50 where ATC = 50. -->

The tax lowers the price toffee makers keep, so each one cuts back and earns a loss. Makers exit until the price they keep is back at minimum ATC. In the long run buyers pay more by the full tax, fewer toffees are sold by fewer makers, and each remaining maker is back where it started, at zero profit.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::: column

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

**Before the tax.** Anyone can make toffee and the number of makers has been constant, so the market is in long-run equilibrium: the price $P_1$ equals minimum ATC, each maker produces where $MC = P_1$, and profit is zero. On the graphs, $P_1 = 50$ at $Q_1 = 50$ thousand, and the maker at $q_1 = 50$ sits at the bottom of its ATC curve.

**The short run.** A per-unit tax raises every maker's cost of selling a toffee by the tax, so the supply curve shifts up by the tax, from $S$ to $S'$. Buyers now pay more ($60$) and sellers keep less: the price a maker keeps falls to $P_2 = 40$, so its flat demand and marginal revenue line drops with it, to $P_2$. Each maker cuts back to where $MC = P_2$, at $q_2 = 40$, where the price it keeps is below ATC ($51.25$): the red box is a loss, $q_2(P_2 - ATC) = 40(40 - 51.25) = -450$. Price is still above AVC, so makers keep operating for now, losing less than their fixed cost.

**The long run.** A loss cannot last in a market anyone can leave. Makers exit, the supply curve shifts in to $S''$, and the price buyers pay rises further ($70$) while the price a maker keeps rises with it. Exit stops when the price a maker keeps is back at $P_3 = P_1 = 50$, minimum ATC, and profit is zero again. Each remaining maker is back at $q_3 = q_1 = 50$, the point of productive efficiency.

**What the tax did.** In the long run the tax raised the price buyers pay by the full tax ($50 \to 70$), shrank the market ($50 \to 30$ thousand toffees) and reduced the number of makers, but left each surviving maker unaffected: the same quantity, zero profit, at the bottom of ATC. The whole burden of the tax lands on buyers because the long-run supply curve of a market with free entry is flat at minimum ATC.

:::::
